etymology: Hebrew Emeq Shaveh, “the valley of the plain”; also called the king’s dale, near Salem, where Melchizedek met Abram returning from battle.
biblical_def: The valley of Shaveh, called the king’s dale, was the place near Salem where the king of Sodom came out to meet Abram as he returned from rescuing Lot and smiting the confederate kings: “And the king of Sodom went out to meet him after his return from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer…at the valley of Shaveh, which is the king’s dale” (Gen 14:17). It was here, in that same dale, that Melchizedek king of Salem, priest of the most high God, brought forth bread and wine and blessed Abram, and Abram gave him tithes of all. The valley preaches the meeting of the two kings and the two kingdoms. The king of Sodom offered Abram the spoils of this world, and Abram refused, that no earthly king might say he had made him rich; but the priest-king Melchizedek gave the blessing of the most high God, possessor of heaven and earth. The valley of Shaveh sets the choice before every soul: the goods of Sodom or the blessing of God, the friendship of the world or the priesthood of Melchizedek. Abram chose the better part, and in Melchizedek beheld a figure of the great High Priest to come, a priest for ever after his order, who blesses His people with bread and wine and the blessing of the most high God, and to whom they render all.

etymology: Hebrew Emeq Berakah, “the valley of blessing”; the place where Jehoshaphat and Judah blessed the LORD after their bloodless victory over Moab and Ammon.
biblical_def: The valley of Berachah, “the valley of blessing,” took its name from a great day of thanksgiving in the reign of Jehoshaphat. When a huge host of Moab, Ammon, and Mount Seir came against Judah, the king set himself to seek the LORD, and the people were told, “the battle is not yours, but God’s.” They went out singing praise, and the LORD set ambushments so that the enemies destroyed one another; Judah had only to gather the spoil. Then, “on the fourth day they assembled themselves in the valley of Berachah; for there they blessed the LORD: therefore the name of the same place was called, The valley of Berachah” (2Ch 20:26). The valley preaches the fitness of praise after deliverance. Judah won by faith and worship, not by the sword, and they did not forget to bless the God who saved them, but gathered on purpose to give thanks. So many are quick to cry to God in trouble and slow to bless Him in deliverance; but the valley of Berachah stands to teach that the mercies of God call for a set and solemn thanksgiving. Let the people of God, having received the victory that is not theirs but His, assemble in their valley of blessing and bless the LORD, whose mercy endureth for ever, and who saveth His people when they praise Him.

etymology: Hebrew Nachal Gerar, “the valley (or brook) of Gerar”; the valley where Isaac dwelt and dug wells; distinct from the city and land of Gerar.
biblical_def: The valley of Gerar was the well-watered vale where Isaac sojourned among the Philistines and dug the wells for which he strove and was blessed: “And Isaac departed thence, and pitched his tent in the valley of Gerar, and dwelt there” (Gen 26:17). This is the valley, distinct from the city and land of Gerar where Abimelech reigned. There Isaac reopened the wells his father Abraham had digged, which the Philistines had stopped with earth, and called them by their old names; and when his herdsmen digged new wells, the men of Gerar strove for the first two, Esek and Sitnah (contention and hatred), but the third he called Rehoboth, “for now the LORD hath made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land” (Gen 26:22). The valley of Gerar preaches patience under strife and the God who makes room for His people. Isaac did not fight for his wells but yielded and moved on, digging again, until God gave him a place of peace and fruitfulness. So the meek inherit the earth; the servant of the LORD strives not, but in patience possesses his soul, and God at last makes room, opening springs of blessing that no adversary can stop. He that will not contend for the wells of this world shall find the LORD digging for him the well of Rehoboth, and making him fruitful in the land.

etymology: Hebrew Emeq Rephaim, “the valley of the giants”; a fertile plain south-west of Jerusalem, scene of David’s victories over the Philistines; distinct from the Rephaim race.
biblical_def: The valley of Rephaim, “the valley of the giants,” was a fruitful plain running south-west from Jerusalem, twice the scene of David’s victories over the Philistines soon after he was made king: “The Philistines also came and spread themselves in the valley of Rephaim” (2Sa 5:18). This is the valley, named after the ancient race of giants, distinct from the Rephaim themselves. When the Philistines came up, David inquired of the LORD, and was told to go up; and he smote them and said, “The LORD hath broken forth upon mine enemies before me, as the breach of waters” (2Sa 5:20), calling the place Baal-perazim. When they came up a second time, David inquired again, and was bidden not to go straight up but to fetch a compass and come upon them over against the mulberry trees, and to move when he heard the sound of a going in the tops of the trees, for then the LORD had gone out before him. The valley preaches the necessity of inquiring of the LORD in every battle, even a battle just won. David did not presume on the former victory nor use the former method the second time, but sought fresh direction and obeyed it exactly. So the believer must seek the LORD anew in each trial, not leaning on past experience nor his own wisdom, but waiting for the sound of the going in the treetops, the sign that God has gone before, and following hard after Him to the victory that is His alone.

etymology: Hebrew Ge Tsephathah, “the valley of watching”; the valley at Mareshah where Asa met the vast host of Zerah the Ethiopian.
biblical_def: The valley of Zephathah was the place at Mareshah, in the low country of Judah, where Asa king of Judah faced the overwhelming host of Zerah the Ethiopian: “Then Asa went out against him, and they set the battle in array in the valley of Zephathah at Mareshah” (2Ch 14:10). Zerah came with a thousand thousand men and three hundred chariots, but Asa cried to the LORD a prayer that has strengthened the faithful ever since: it is nothing with Thee to help, whether with many, or with them that have no power; help us, O LORD our God, for we rest on Thee, and in Thy name we go against this multitude. And the LORD smote the Ethiopians, and they fled and were destroyed. The valley of Zephathah preaches the power of humble faith against impossible odds. Asa did not trust his own numbers but leaned wholly on the LORD, confessing that God can save as easily by the weak as by the strong, and resting his whole cause on the divine name. So the believer, facing a multitude of enemies within and without, may cry the same prayer and find the same help; for the LORD delights to show Himself strong on behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward Him, and it is nothing with Him to save by many or by few.

etymology: Hebrew Ge ha-Tseboim, “the valley of hyenas”; a ravine in Benjamin toward the wilderness, on the way of the Philistine raiders; distinct from Zeboiim of the cities of the plain.
biblical_def: The valley of Zeboim, “the valley of hyenas,” was a ravine in the territory of Benjamin, running down toward the wilderness, named as one of the ways taken by the Philistine spoilers in the days of Saul: “another company turned to the way of the border that looketh to the valley of Zeboim toward the wilderness” (1Sa 13:18). This is a place, distinct from Zeboiim, one of the cities of the plain destroyed with Sodom. The Philistines had so subdued Israel that they sent out raiding bands in three directions, wasting the land, while Israel had no smith and scarcely a sword, for the enemy had disarmed them. The valley of the hyenas, haunt of the scavenging beast, is a fit emblem of that desolate and defenceless time. It preaches the wretchedness of a people brought low by long unfaithfulness, stripped of weapons and overrun by their foes. Yet even in that dark hour the LORD had not forsaken His people; He was raising up Jonathan’s faith and preparing a deliverance. The valley of Zeboim reminds the church that her lowest estate, when the enemy ranges freely and she seems disarmed and helpless, is not beyond the reach of God, who can turn the tide by a single believing heart and save His people when they have no might of their own.

etymology: Hebrew Ge Charashim, “the valley of craftsmen”; a valley near Lod and Ono, inhabited by craftsmen; also called the valley of craftsmen after the exile.
biblical_def: The valley of Charashim, “the valley of craftsmen,” was a place near Lod and Ono, so named because its inhabitants were artificers and skilled workmen: “Joab, the father of the valley of Charashim; for they were craftsmen” (1Ch 4:14). After the exile the returning Benjamites dwelt there again, at Lod, Ono, and the valley of craftsmen. The valley preaches the dignity of honest craft and the place of the skilled hand in the purposes of God. Scripture does not despise the labour of the craftsman; the LORD Himself filled Bezaleel and Aholiab with the Spirit of God in wisdom and understanding to work all manner of cunning work for the tabernacle, and the Lord Jesus laboured as a carpenter in Nazareth. The valley of the craftsmen honours those who work faithfully with their hands, and reminds the church that God is glorified not only in the pulpit and the field but at the bench and the forge. Every lawful calling, wrought skilfully and unto the Lord, is a service to Him; whatsoever the hand findeth to do is to be done with the might, as unto the LORD and not unto men. The valley of craftsmen bids the workman labour heartily at his trade, knowing that of the Lord he shall receive the reward, for he serves the Lord Christ.

etymology: Hebrew Emeq Yizreel, “the valley of Jezreel” (“God soweth”); the great plain of the north, scene of many of Israel’s battles.
biblical_def: The valley of Jezreel, whose name means “God soweth,” was the great and fertile plain of the north, stretching between Galilee and Samaria, and the scene of many decisive battles in Israel’s history. There Gideon and his three hundred faced the Midianites who “pitched in the valley of Jezreel” (Judg 6:33); there Saul and his sons fell before the Philistines on the slopes of Gilboa; and there the LORD declared judgment on the bloody house of Ahab and Jezebel. Through Hosea the LORD said, “I will break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel” (Hos 1:5), for the sowing of God is both to judgment and to mercy. The great plain preaches the certainty of harvest according to sowing. Its very name declares that God soweth; and whatsoever a man or a nation soweth, that shall he also reap. Israel sowed the wind of idolatry and reaped the whirlwind of judgment in that valley of blood. Yet the same name of Jezreel was turned to mercy, for the LORD promised a day when He would sow His people unto Himself in the earth, and say to them which were not His people, Thou art my people. The valley of Jezreel bids every soul consider what it sows, for the God who soweth will surely bring in the harvest, to judgment for the impenitent, but to everlasting mercy for those He sows unto Himself.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. A great battle-plain raises no modern quarrel. Its name, “God soweth,” and its long history of battles turn the mind to the certain harvest that follows sowing.

The principle to recover is that God brings in the harvest according to the sowing. Its very name declares that God soweth; and whatsoever a man or a nation soweth, that shall he reap. Israel sowed the wind of idolatry and reaped the whirlwind of judgment in that valley of blood. Yet the name was turned to mercy, for God promised to sow His people unto Himself and call them His people. Consider what thou sowest, for the God who soweth will surely bring in the harvest.

etymology: Hebrew Ge Hamon Gog, “the valley of the multitude of Gog”; the place of the burial of Gog and his host in Ezekiel’s prophecy.
biblical_def: The valley of Hamon-gog, “the multitude of Gog,” is a place named in Ezekiel’s prophecy of the overthrow of Gog, the great enemy who comes up against the people of God in the latter days: “I will give unto Gog a place there of graves in Israel…and there shall they bury Gog and all his multitude: and they shall call it The valley of Hamongog” (Eze 39:11). Gog gathers a vast host against the LORD’s people, but God Himself overthrows him utterly, so that his multitude fills a valley of graves, and seven months are spent burying the slain, that the land may be cleansed. The valley preaches the certain and final destruction of the last enemies of God and His church. However great the multitude that gathers against the Lord and His anointed, the end is a valley of graves; the LORD will be known by the judgment which He executeth, and the heathen shall know that He is the LORD. This is the sure hope of the church in every age of persecution: the enemy may come up as a cloud to cover the land, but his end is appointed, and God shall get Himself the victory and the glory. The valley of Hamon-gog is a standing pledge that every uprising against the kingdom of Christ ends in the grave, and that the LORD reigns, and His people are safe, when all the multitudes of Gog are brought down to the dust.

etymology: Hebrew Har Gaash, “quaking mountain”; a hill in mount Ephraim, on whose north side Timnath-serah lay, where Joshua was buried.
biblical_def: Mount Gaash, the “quaking mountain,” was a hill in the mountain country of Ephraim, remembered because near it was buried the great captain of Israel: “And they buried him in the border of his inheritance in Timnathserah, which is in mount Ephraim, on the north side of the hill of Gaash” (Josh 24:30); so also in Judges, “on the north side of the hill Gaash” (Judg 2:9). There Joshua the son of Nun, who had led Israel into the land and divided the inheritance, was laid to rest in his own portion, having served his generation by the will of God. Mount Gaash preaches the passing of the servants and the abiding of the LORD. Joshua died, and was buried by the quaking mountain, and after him arose a generation that knew not the LORD nor the works He had done for Israel; and the people forsook the God of their fathers. The grave by Mount Gaash marks the end of an age of faithfulness and the beginning of decline, a warning that the mightiest servant of God is mortal, and that each generation must know the LORD for itself, not resting on the faith of the fathers. Joshua rested from his labours in his inheritance, as all the faithful shall; but the LORD who buried His servant lives for ever, and raises up in every age new labourers for His unchanging work.
